title: What sautéing does to your veggies

beats.vo: Oil helps your carrots. Heat can cost your peppers.
beats.visual: Overhead on a warm countertop: a pile of matte, chunky orange carrot coins on the left, red pepper strips on the right, a cast-iron pan between them. Soft window light. Reads in under 2 s.

beats.vo: One pan. Two opposite things happening to your veggies.
beats.visual: Straight overhead push-in on the pan as a ribbon of oil slides in; Tomato-red heat shimmer rises on the right half. Motivated by the oil pour.

beats.vo: Bright veggies like carrots are full of plant pigments called carotenoids. Your body turns them into vitamin A.
beats.visual: Overhead on a carrot coin; camera drops straight down into the orange flesh to a field of glowing orange pigment molecules, then a soft arrow turns them into a small 'A' tile.

beats.vo: Here's the catch. Those pigments get absorbed better with a little fat.
beats.visual: Two molecule panels on plant cells: pigments sliding past the gut lining with no oil vs wrapped in golden oil droplets that dock into the lining (labels: no oil / with oil).

beats.vo: Think of it like a ride. The pigments travel along with the oil.
beats.visual: Oil droplets carry orange molecules like little buses along the surface; side-lit by warm light. Camera glides slowly along the path (follow).

beats.vo: So a splash of oil isn't just for flavor.
beats.visual: Pull back up out of the molecule scale to the overhead pan; oil glints around the carrot coins as they brown.

beats.vo: Same story for vitamins E and K, in spinach and broccoli. Fat helps them in.
beats.visual: Overhead over spinach and broccoli hitting the pan; E and K tiles land beside them, the A tile stays with the carrots.

beats.vo: Now the flip side. Peppers, broccoli and tomatoes are packed with vitamin C.
beats.visual: Overhead tilt-free pan to the side where red pepper strips, broccoli and a cut tomato sit on the board; a bright Herb-green 'C' tile pops above them.

beats.vo: Vitamin C dissolves in water, and cooking can lower how much is left.
beats.visual: Camera drops into a pepper strip: Herb-green C molecules floating in watery cells; heat shimmer arrives and a few of them fade out.

beats.vo: Microwaving and steaming can lower it too, so it's not just the pan.
beats.visual: Hard cut on 'Microwaving' to an overhead trio: pan, steamer basket, microwave plate, each with the same partial dim on its C tiles, tagged 'illustration, not to scale'. Nothing is removed, no order is implied.

beats.vo: That's why raw fruit and veg top the vitamin C lists.
beats.visual: Overhead, hard cut: a raw bell pepper (left) and a sautéed one (right), each with the same six C tiles; the cooked set dims to the same partial level as the trio. Tag: illustration, not to scale. No move.

beats.vo: So sautéing isn't good or bad. It's a trade.
beats.visual: Real kitchen scale (flat dish on a counter) with two small plates: raw peppers on one, sautéed carrots on the other, settling level. Slow overhead push-in.

beats.vo: This isn't a diet rule. It's just what your pan is doing.
beats.visual: Back to the full overhead pan, veggies browning, steam curling up. Hold steady.

beats.vo: The Pan Theory: carrots want a little oil. Peppers can keep more C raw.
beats.visual: Signature card on the Countertop beige: 'The Pan Theory:' in Rubik with Tomato-red key word, two Butter lines below. Food education, not diet advice.

end_card.text: The Pan Theory: carrots want a little oil. Peppers can keep more C raw.
